units.title: Saying no
units.goal: Turn any sentence into its negative, two ways.
explain: Put 안 directly in front of the verb and the sentence becomes negative: 가요 I go, 안 가요 I don't go. Short, spoken, everywhere.

The longer way puts 지 않아요 on the end of the stem instead: 가지 않아요. It means exactly the same thing but sounds more considered — you meet it in writing, in notices and in the exam far more often than in the canteen.
One trap: verbs built from a noun plus 하다 split apart. 일하다 becomes 일 안 해요, not 안 일해요. The 안 goes in front of 해요, because 하다 is the verb and 일 is just a noun sitting in front of it.

examples.en: This machine isn't in use right now.

notes: 있다 and 알다 have their own negative words — 없다 and 모르다. 안 있어요 and 안 알아요 are wrong.
못 is different from 안. 안 가요 means I don't go, by choice. 못 가요 means I can't go, something is stopping me. Getting these two backwards changes a preference into an obstacle.

exercises.why: 안 goes directly in front of the verb.
Noun + 하다 verbs split: the 안 goes in front of 해요.

exercises.q: Your shift ends late so you cannot come. Which do you say?
exercises.why: 못 is for when something prevents you. 안 would suggest you simply chose not to.

pairs.note: 안 sits in front of the verb and nothing else changes. It is the short, spoken negative.
The same meaning by a longer road. 지 않다 is the one you will see in writing and on the exam paper; 안 is the one you will hear.

units.title: Talking about what already happened
units.goal: Report your day — what you did, where you went, when you arrived.
explain: The past is one block, 았 or 었, slipped in between the stem and the ending. Choose it exactly the way you chose 아요/어요 in Level 1: stem vowel ㅏ or ㅗ takes 았어요, everything else takes 었어요, and 하다 becomes 했어요.
Korean uses the past far more readily than English does. 밥 먹었어요? is the normal greeting for have you eaten, and 알았어요 is what you say to mean understood, right now, in this moment.
There is no separate perfect tense. 갔어요 covers went, has gone and had gone. Context carries the difference, and a time word usually does the work: 어제 갔어요, 벌써 갔어요.

examples.en: I came to Korea last year.
My wages haven't come in yet.

notes: 알겠어요 and 알았어요 both mean got it. 알겠어요 is softer and more common at work when a supervisor tells you something.
Watch the contractions: 오다 becomes 왔어요, 보다 becomes 봤어요, 주다 becomes 줬어요, 하다 becomes 했어요. Same squashing as the present tense.

exercises.why: 하다 becomes 했어요 in the past.

exercises.qEn: I came to Korea last year.
My wages haven't come in yet.

exercises.why: Stem vowel ㅓ is not ㅏ or ㅗ, so 었어요.

pairs.note: 었 slots in between the stem and the ending. The ending you already know does not change — it just gets pushed along.
가 + 았어요 contracts to 갔어요. Korean swallows the repeated vowel rather than saying it twice.

units.title: Wanting, and joining two things
units.goal: Say what you want, and put two sentences together without stopping.
explain: Add 고 싶어요 to a verb stem and you have I want to: 가고 싶어요 I want to go, 쉬고 싶어요 I want to rest. The stem never changes shape for this one, which makes it a relief after the last two units.

There is a catch that native speakers apply without thinking: you do not use 고 싶어요 about someone else. For a third person Korean switches to 고 싶어 해요 — 동생이 가고 싶어 해요, my younger sibling wants to go. Korean treats another person's inner wants as something you can only observe, not state.
The same 고 on its own links two clauses: and, or and then. 밥을 먹고 일해요 — I eat and then work. It is the workhorse joiner of spoken Korean.

examples.en: I want to learn more Korean.
My friend wants to go back home.

notes: 하고 joins nouns and is the spoken one. 와 and 과 are the written pair — 와 after a vowel, 과 after a consonant. Do not use 고 between two nouns.
For the thing you want, both 을/를 and 이/가 are heard: 물을 마시고 싶어요 and 물이 마시고 싶어요 are both said. Neither is wrong.

exercises.why: 고 싶어요 attaches straight to the stem 가.

exercises.qEn: My friend wants to go home.
exercises.why: For someone else's wants, Korean uses 고 싶어 해요.

exercises.qEn: I want to learn more Korean.

exercises.why: Between two nouns you need 하고, not 고.

pairs.note: 고 싶다 attaches to the stem and turns a statement into a wish. Note it describes YOUR wish — for someone else's you need 고 싶어하다.
고 welds two verbs into one sentence, so you stop needing 그리고 between every pair of clauses.

units.title: Telling someone politely to do something
units.goal: Give an instruction, and understand the ones shouted at you on the floor.
explain: (으)세요 does two jobs with one shape. Said to you it is a polite instruction — 앉으세요 please sit, 여기 쓰세요 write here. Said about someone senior it is the respectful form of the verb — 사장님이 지금 오세요, the boss is coming.
Consonant stem takes 으세요, vowel stem takes 세요. The ㄹ at the end of a stem drops out first: 만들다 becomes 만드세요.
A handful of verbs swap for a different word entirely in the respectful form, and they are the common ones: 먹다 becomes 드세요, 자다 becomes 주무세요, 있다 becomes 계세요, 말하다 becomes 말씀하세요.
notes: Never use (으)세요 about yourself. 저는 가세요 is wrong — you are being respectful to yourself. It is 저는 가요.
안녕히 가세요 is said to whoever is leaving; 안녕히 계세요 is said to whoever is staying. If you both leave, you both say 가세요.
The negative instruction is 지 마세요: 들어가지 마세요 do not enter, 만지지 마세요 do not touch. You will see both on signs.

exercises.why: 쓰 ends in a vowel, so 세요.
먹다 swaps for 드시다 in the respectful form.

exercises.q: You are leaving the office; your colleague is staying. What do you say to them?
exercises.why: 계세요 is said to the one who stays.

pairs.aEn: I sit here. / You sit here.
pairs.note: 아요/어요 only states. 으세요 asks, politely, and is what you will be spoken to in all day.

pairs.bEn: Please look at this for me.
pairs.note: 세요 is a polite instruction. Add 주다 and it becomes a favour — see unit 12.

units.title: Plans and the future
units.goal: Say what you are going to do — tomorrow, next month, when the contract ends.
explain: (으)ㄹ 거예요 is the plain future: I will, I'm going to. Vowel stem takes ㄹ 거예요 glued straight on, consonant stem takes 을 거예요.
It also carries a guess about someone else. 사장님이 화날 거예요 means the boss will probably be angry — you are predicting, not announcing. The context tells a listener which of the two you mean.
Remember that 아/어요 already handles the near future. 지금 갈 거예요 and 지금 가요 are both fine for leaving in a minute. Save 거예요 for plans with some distance in them.

examples.en: I'm going to rest at the weekend.
My contract will end next month.

notes: In speech it is usually squashed to 거예요 → 거에요 → 껄, and you will hear 갈 거예요 as gal-kkeoyeyo. The ㄹ makes the next consonant tense.
(으)ㄹ게요 is a near neighbour with a different flavour: it is a promise to the person you are speaking to. 제가 할게요 — I'll do it, leave it to me. Do not use 을게요 for weather or for other people.

exercises.why: 가 ends in a vowel, so ㄹ 거예요.
먹 ends in a consonant, so 을 거예요.

exercises.qEn: My contract will end next month.

options: I'm going to rest at the weekend.
Do you rest at the weekend?

exercises.q: Your supervisor asks who will clean the machine. You volunteer. Which fits best?
exercises.why: (으)ㄹ게요 is a promise made to the person in front of you.

pairs.note: ㄹ 거예요 is the plain future: what you intend, what will happen. Said quickly it sounds like 일할 꺼예요, which is correct pronunciation, not sloppiness.

pairs.bEn: I'm going to take tomorrow off.
pairs.note: Korean often uses the present for a fixed future arrangement, exactly as English does with I'm off tomorrow. 거예요 adds intention.

units.title: Asking for a favour
units.goal: Ask someone to do something for you — the single most useful pattern in this course.
explain: Take the 아/어 form you learned in Level 1, drop the 요, and add 주세요. 하다 becomes 해 주세요, 쓰다 becomes 써 주세요, 가르치다 becomes 가르쳐 주세요. It means please do it for me, and the for me is the point — 주다 is the verb to give.

Compare it with the last unit. 쓰세요 is an instruction: write it. 써 주세요 is a request: please write it for me. One is what a supervisor says to you; the other is what you say to a supervisor. Mixing them up is the most common politeness mistake foreign workers make in their first year.
좀 slipped in front softens it further. Literally it means a little, but its real job is to take the edge off: 좀 도와주세요 — could you help me.

examples.en: Please speak a little more slowly.
Please take me to the hospital.

notes: 주세요 on its own goes after a noun and means please give me: 물 주세요, 영수증 주세요. No verb needed.
For someone clearly senior, 주시겠어요? or 주시겠습니까? is one step more formal — could you possibly. Keep it for 사장님 and for offices.
These five sentences are worth memorising before you can build them. 다시 말해 주세요 and 천천히 말해 주세요 will carry you through every conversation you do not understand, which for a while is most of them.

exercises.q: Your supervisor is writing a note. You want a copy written for you. Which do you say?
exercises.why: 써 주세요 asks them to do it for you. 쓰세요 orders them to write.

exercises.qEn: Please speak a little more slowly.

exercises.why: After a noun, 주세요 alone means please give me.

pairs.note: 아/어 주다 says the action is done FOR somebody. Leaving it out is the difference between describing and asking.
Both are polite; 주세요 is warmer, because it admits the other person is doing you a kindness. Use it when you are the one who needs something.
